rows.title: Top strategist says a ‘surprise’ rate cut could be coming next month—and it’s because Trump is leading in the polls
rows.standfirst: Société Générale’s Albert Edwards knows he’s in “tricky territory” discussing the role politics plays in Fed policy, but he has “a few observations” to share.

rows.title: Luxury home prices are hitting all-time highs, too, and all-cash bids are driving up the market, Redfin finds
rows.standfirst: “Luxury prices are rising at twice the rate of non-luxury prices largely because so many affluent buyers are able to buy homes in cash.”

rows.title: Most American adults don’t have enough savings to pay an emergency $1,000 expense
rows.standfirst: Bankrate’s Mark Hamrick tells Fortune that it’s “disappointing because it is an indication that so many Americans are living paycheck to paycheck.”

rows.title: Once-unstoppable consumers are finally tapping the brakes—and Adidas, Nike, and Puma are taking a beating from sinking sales
rows.standfirst: “It’s not like people are lining up everywhere to buy product,” one CEO said.

rows.title: Housing inequality: Black homeowners won’t catch up at this rate for over 300 years. But they could with a $1.7 trillion affordable housing plan, McKinsey says
rows.standfirst: But they could with a $1.7 trillion to $2.4 trillion affordable housing plan over two decades, McKinsey says.

rows.title: Europe’s largest airline is getting into the landlord business because its new hires can’t find housing amid Dublin’s rent crisis
rows.standfirst: “This accommodation, which is located one bus stop from Dublin Airport, will be rented at affordable rates to Ryanair cabin crew,” a spokesperson told Fortune.

rows.title: Why is rent still so high, a year after experts told us it was going to fall?
rows.standfirst: Housing inflation has been slow to come down, despite even Jerome Powell saying it would. But the government’s measurement of it is weird.

rows.title: American exceptionalism is real—in the stock market
rows.standfirst: American exceptionalism may or may not be real when it comes to politics, but it certainly is when it comes to markets.

rows.title: Jerome Powell says remote work ‘looks like it’ll be a persistent thing’
rows.standfirst: But the Federal Reserve chair told “60 Minutes” that “the jury is out” on how frequent or prevalent remote work will be.

rows.title: Texas lawmaker who opposes giving $500 per month to 1,900 Houstonians sponsored a bill to save every homeowner $1,300 a year
rows.standfirst: “We just can’t hand out money like popcorn on street corners to people that walk by,” State Sen. Paul Bettencourt told Fox News.

rows.title: Goldman’s strategy guru says we’ve begun a rocky ‘post-modern’ cycle in the world economy—and AI could save the day from raging conflict, higher rates, and surging deficits
rows.standfirst: Peter Oppenheimer’s new book, “Any Happy Returns,” charts the multi-decade cycles we’ve just come through, and he previewed what’s up next for Fortune.

rows.title: Thank America’s immigrants for killing the recession and keeping unemployment at 50-year lows, Nobel laureate Paul Krugman says
rows.standfirst: America managed to achieve a “soft landing” thanks to an immigration rebound, says Nobel laureate Paul Krugman.

rows.title: Breaking down the costs of your Super Bowl feast—it’s a good year to have wings
rows.standfirst: Chips? Not so much.

rows.title: First National Bank caught ignoring Black, Latino neighborhoods in North Carolina as redlining mortgage scandal grows
rows.standfirst: This is the 13th redlining settlement that the Biden Administration has brought against banks since 2021.

rows.title: Jerome Powell is vague on rate cuts because he’s ‘petrified’ of repeating the mistakes of one predecessor, says ‘Big Short’ investor Steve Eisman
rows.standfirst: Eisman argued that the Fed can already “declare victory” over inflation and that it has “engineered something really pretty fantastic.”

rows.title: America’s falling out of love with its California dream—and housing costs are a major reason why, report says
rows.standfirst: “The real story, arguably, is the decline in the share of population of the West … Its share of overall U.S. population has flattened, and now appears to be falling,” Bank of America said in a new research note.

rows.title: Falling inflation and a growing economy aren’t convincing worried voters: ‘I feel like there’s a recession and I’m living it’
rows.standfirst: Biden is telling voters that the numbers point to a brighter future, while Trump says the gains are merely the fumes of his time in office.

rows.title: Danish wind giant’s abysmal 3 months have a lot to do with America, ‘the most painful’ part of its portfolio
rows.standfirst: “We now have a new plan in place that will more than double Orsted’s capacity by the end of the decade,” Orsted’s chair said when announcing the overhaul.

rows.title: Meet Zillow rooms for rent: A Craigslist killer for the millennial and Gen Z set—and a symbol of the housing affordability crisis
rows.standfirst: Landlords can list single rooms through Zillow’s new rooms for rent feature.

rows.title: Boomers believe they don’t have enough money to retire. Signs point to them being, sadly, right
rows.standfirst: Battling inflation and living longer, some retirees haven’t saved anything at all.

rows.title: ‘Disenfranchised’ millennials feel ‘locked out’ of the housing market and it taints every part of economic life, top economist Mark Zandi says
rows.standfirst: “If they feel like they’re locked out of owning a home, it colors their perceptions about everything else going on in their financial lives,” Zandi says.

rows.title: With the whole world waiting for the Fed to cut rates, official says ‘history tells many stories of inflation head-fakes’
rows.standfirst: Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin, in a speech Thursday, noted a 1986 surge after Paul Volcker cut rates. “I would love to avoid that roller-coaster if we can.”

rows.title: Gen Z grad with 2 degrees breaks down in tears sharing the responses she received from minimum wage employers after handing out her résumé in New York
rows.standfirst: “This is the most humbled I’ve ever felt in my life,” the teary-eyed Gen Z graduate reported back to her TikTok fans after a disappointing day of job-seeking.

rows.title: Here’s why the slowest rent growth in 14 years isn’t what it looks like—and you’ll get a good deal if you’re wealthy
rows.standfirst: The rental market is really only interested in a certain demographic, according to a report by Yardi Matrix.

rows.title: Airbnb investor rips South Lake Tahoe short-term rental ban, saying it just lets ‘wealthy people get good deals on second homes that mostly sit around vacant’
rows.standfirst: “There is still a housing affordability crisis,” says Rohin Dhar of the Northern California resort’s “short-term rental Armageddon.”

rows.title: Gen Z’s thirst for the NYC lifestyle drives vacancy rates to the historic low of 1.4%—unseen since the ‘Mad Men’ era of 1968
rows.standfirst: “The data is clear: The demand to live in our city is far outpacing our ability to build housing,” New York City Mayor Eric Adams says.

rows.title: IKEA’s price cuts come from a cocktail of automation, low raw material costs and ‘saving for the rainy days’
rows.standfirst: “It’s time for us to really double down to do the opposite of what is expected,” Ikea-owner Ingka Group’s Tolga Öncü said.

rows.title: Asia’s fastest inflation just got a political crisis as Pakistan’s middle class throws majority to jailed Imran Khan’s party
rows.standfirst: Analysts say the nation’s powerful military is backing a status quo government of parties backed by the Sharif and Bhutto clans.

rows.title: Europe’s economic crisis has obliterated Gen Z and millennial drinking habits—and it might be kicking off a long-term sobriety movement
rows.standfirst: A third of Europe’s young people spent less on alcohol last year as the continent flirted with recession. Not many are planning to return to booze.

rows.title: Here’s how the U.S., Europe, and China are faring in the post-pandemic race for economic growth
rows.standfirst: Three charts compare GDP growth to pre-pandemic trends in the world’s largest economies.

rows.title: Everybody hates inflation–even grocers
rows.standfirst: 77% of grocery shoppers say they compare prices across stores, more than any other retail category.

rows.title: A Florida family that bought a fishing cottage for $1 million in the 1980s is selling it for $295 million now that it’s a 20-bedroom compound with its own yacht basin
rows.standfirst: The deceased owner’s 13 children have decided it’s “more or less” time to sell.

rows.title: Shrinkflation is so rampant Biden had to step in with a PSA before the Super Bowl telling companies to cut it out. ‘The American public is tired of being played for suckers’
rows.standfirst: President Joe Biden blamed companies for many of the high prices Americans still see at the grocery store.

rows.title: Meet the worst offenders on ‘shrinkflation’: dollar stores
rows.standfirst: It might feel cheaper to shop at your local dollar store, but you usually get a better deal at Walmart or Target.

rows.title: Elon Musk weighs in on U.S. national debt debate, joining the likes of Jamie Dimon and Jerome Powell in expressing concern about the $34 trillion Uncle Sam owes
rows.standfirst: The Tesla CEO was responding to monthly Treasury data showing the government’s $357 billion in interest payments easily eclipsed spending on the country’s military.

rows.title: Inflation fails to fall below 3%, disappointing economic forecasts
rows.standfirst: Inflation in January fell to 3.1%, from 3.4% in December, but economists were expecting to see 2.9%.

rows.title: Congress could be about to give grocery stores and gas stations new payment options—but big banks are warning the savings will not be passed on to consumers and could mean the end of credit card rewards
rows.standfirst: The Electronic Payments Coalition, of which Visa and Mastercard are members, says the savings will benefit grocery and gas station chains, not consumers.

rows.title: AI is leading to job losses, but not in the way people feared
rows.standfirst: It is the cost of AI, not its capability, that is putting people out of work, while in other cases CEOs simply aren’t telling the truth about layoffs.

rows.title: CEO of a $19 billion U.K. bank with business in Hong Kong since the Victorian age sees a ‘lack of confidence’ unraveling China’s economy
rows.standfirst: Standard Chartered has had a branch in Hong Kong since 1859, and 90% of its profits come from outside the U.K.

rows.title: Americans are judging the economy ‘more harshly’ due to politics and an over 15% ‘perceived inflation’ peak, Goldman Sachs says
rows.standfirst: The Wall Street economist who predicted the U.S. would avoid a recession says “partisan bias” is playing a role in American attitudes.

rows.title: McDonald’s CEO sees a McFlation ‘battleground’ with customers revolting over $8 chicken sandwiches and $3 hash browns
rows.standfirst: “I think what you’re going to see as you head into 2024 is probably more attention to what I would describe as affordability,” CEO Chris Kempczinski said.

rows.title: Wall Street’s winning streak shattered on ‘sticky’ inflation data as Dow falls over 500 points from record high
rows.standfirst: The hotter-than-expected inflation report may have put the final nail into hopes that the first cut could arrive in March.

rows.title: Inflation is no match for AI, top analyst says: ‘We’re at the start of a 3- to 5-year tech bull market’
rows.standfirst: The Labor Department’s latest report indicates inflation was slightly hotter than expected in January.

rows.title: The stock market just threw a tantrum—here’s why
rows.standfirst: It’s a “wake-up call,” says top economist Mohamed El-Erian, adding the market got “carried away, without much critical thinking, about a very soft landing.”

rows.title: The comfort of 4,000 people in one of California’s wealthiest towns outweighs a rail project connecting San Diego to the country, some residents say
rows.standfirst: “Del Mar residents should not have to put up with the vibration and dangers of tunneling under their homes,” a local wrote to the City Council.

rows.title: Bud Light isn’t the only beer brand struggling: Gen Z’s prohibition vibes are souring the future of beer as we know it
rows.standfirst: Brewers are waking up to the fact that Gen Z just isn’t that into them.

rows.title: Gen Z’s cost of living–induced sobriety drive is forcing U.K. nightclubs to shut, owner says
rows.standfirst: Young students don’t have the time or money to go clubbing, and it’s led nearly a third of clubs to shut since the pandemic began.

rows.title: The U.K. and Japan have slumped into recession while the U.S. keeps defying gloomy expectations
rows.standfirst: Several unique characteristics of the U.S. economy have sheltered it from recessionary storms, analysts say.

rows.title: The U.K. just entered a recession—but a surprise boost from strong retail sales could be the glimmer of hope its economy needed
rows.standfirst: Though one economist warned that “January’s bounce should be taken with just as much of a pinch of salt as December’s fall.”

rows.title: Wholesale prices jumped in January, the latest sign inflation remains stubbornly sticky: ‘The Fed will be concerned’
rows.standfirst: The producer price index — which tracks inflation before it reaches consumers — rose 0.3% in January after falling the month before.

rows.title: Walmart has been eating Target’s lunch and now the Minnesota giant is ditching its ‘Tar-jay’ rep for a ‘Hail Mary’ budget brand mostly priced under $10
rows.standfirst: “We know that value is top of mind for consumers,” says Target EVP Rick Gomez of the new dealworthy line, “backed by our owned brand promise.”

rows.title: Did Wall Street kill the American Dream of homeownership? It depends on where you live
rows.standfirst: Institutional investors can’t be blamed for the housing crisis that’s unfolded across the country. But so-called desirable markets like Atlanta, Dallas, and Charlotte tell a different story.

rows.title: The Chip Wars continue: GlobalFoundries scores $1.5 billion to fund expansion in New York, Vermont
rows.standfirst: The chipmaker is the latest to see a funding infusion as part of Biden’s CHIPS and Science Act.

rows.title: 3 reasons why we aren’t in a housing emergency, according to an official at the center of the 2008 financial crisis
rows.standfirst: “Every crisis is different, and we’re not in a crisis now,” James B. Lockhart III said.

rows.title: Top economist ‘very worried’ about America’s $34 trillion national debts: ‘There’s absolutely no attempt to decrease them in any way, shape or form’
rows.standfirst: Former IMF chief economist Olivier Blanchard talked to the House of Lords Economic Affairs Committee via video link on Tuesday.

rows.title: Black, Hispanic homebuyers pay higher interest rates on average, even as ownership levels hit new peaks
rows.standfirst: For loans originated in 2022, a fifth of Black and Hispanic buyers paid interest rates of 6% or more, higher than that of Asian and white borrowers.

rows.title: Robots and AI are saving the American economy with a boom in productivity, the ‘magic beanstalk beans’ that allow higher wages without inflation
rows.standfirst: Chronic worker shortages have led many companies to invest in machines to do some of the work they can’t find people to do.

rows.title: Millennials and Gen Zers are worried about outliving their savings and are turning to hot-stock tips. But a comprehensive retirement plan drives better outcomes
rows.standfirst: Stark societal and economic realities have many millennials and Gen Zers turning to social media “experts” for financial guidance.

rows.title: Bank of America CEO Brian Moynihan explains why you’d better ‘get used to mortgage rates of six, seven percent’
rows.standfirst: “Pricing went up, and wages went up,” the Bank of America CEO told CNBC at a Miami investor conference. “They just went up in two different cycles.”

rows.title: Say goodbye to the peak of home price appreciation, Fortune 500 chief economist says—it’s behind us
rows.standfirst: Home prices rose for 10 months straight, but Mark Fleming, chief economist at First American, sees a change.

rows.title: Buyers line up overnight for a chance to snap up luxury waterfront homes in one of the world’s hottest property markets
rows.standfirst: The project on Dubai Islands have prices starting at $1.2 million apiece, with the most expensive properties will cost upwards of $4 million.

rows.title: Nestle made big gains when high inflation gave it a reason to charge consumers more. But as prices level, the Nespresso maker says growth is set to cool
rows.standfirst: Nestle shares fell as much as 5.3% to the lowest level in almost four years, while Danone rose as much as 3.4%.

rows.title: Global trade is at a critical juncture–and we can’t take it for granted, WTO meeting chair warns
rows.standfirst: The WTO and the treaties that make up the bedrock of international trade are being buffeted by powerful political forces and new technologies.

rows.title: ‘What’s the rush?’ The Fed’s last meeting had a lot of talk dousing Wall Street’s hopes for rate cuts
rows.standfirst: “We need to verify that the progress on inflation we saw in the last half of 2023 will continue and this means there is no rush,” Christopher Waller said.

rows.title: Million-dollar homes are swallowing D.C.’s housing market as a whopping 20% of listings are out of reach for most people
rows.standfirst: Most D.C. residents can only afford a $300,000 home

rows.title: Oregon is so green because it’s been literally illegal to build housing outside cities since the 1970s. That could be changing
rows.standfirst: Without the 1970s-era law on the urban growth boundary, “All that farmland would likely be a sea of strip malls and subdivisions.”

rows.title: ‘Consumers are more powerful than President Biden’: The war on greedflation is being won one private-label brand at a time
rows.standfirst: Stuart Dryden, a 37-year-old in Virginia, says he’s been trying private-label groceries: “the quality is the same and it’s almost a no-brainer to switch.”

rows.title: Remember the predicted 2024 recession? Economists don’t—they’ve instead raised their growth forecast by almost 70% for the year
rows.standfirst: Economists also more than doubled their estimates for the number of jobs gained across the economy this year, though it would still likely be down from the previous one.

rows.title: We asked 50,000 citizens in 23 countries what they expect of their government–70% of those in developed nations say theirs is not doing enough to address inflation and the high cost of living
rows.standfirst: the chasm between citizens’ expectations and governments’ delivery is widening.

rows.title: Washington, D.C.’s hip U Street neighborhood hates a high-rise conversion that hasn’t even been started yet
rows.standfirst: “They want to build a massive building,” a longtime resident told Fortune. “It’s too big, it’s too high, it’s too dense.”

rows.title: Wells Fargo study highlights increasing anxiety among U.S. earners: ‘We’re not getting as much utility out of our money as we used to’
rows.standfirst: “We’re moving into this domain where money isn’t viewed as a tool or agent to prosperity, it’s viewed as something that is very limited and that needs to be held close.”

rows.title: The whole world’s economy can actually pull off a soft landing, G-20 says
rows.standfirst: “We note that the likelihood of a soft landing in the global economy has increased,” says a draft of the G-20’s closing statement seen by Bloomberg.

rows.title: A wealthy doctor refuses to leave his $16 million mansion even though it could fall into the Pacific Ocean
rows.standfirst: “The house is fine,” Dr. Lewis Bruggeman told a local CBS station. “It’s not threatened. It will not be red-tagged.”

rows.title: The sky-high cost of food is eating up our paychecks at a near-historic rate
rows.standfirst: The cost of food remains stubbornly high despite ebbing inflation.

rows.title: Florida homeowners have no choice but to lower condo prices as insurance and HOA fees ‘skyrocket,’ Redfin says
rows.standfirst: Condo prices in Florida are dropping while the U.S. average continues to rise.

rows.title: Mass. gov. rips ‘decades of inertia and inaction’ as she pitches $4 billion housing fix: ‘There’s a reason people think about North Carolina or Texas’
rows.standfirst: “Housing is the biggest challenge we face,” Maura Healey said. “We’ve been down 200,000 housing units in our state.”

rows.title: Blame the Fed’s inflation fighting for why Americans are miserable about the economy, according to Larry Summers (and a bunch of other top economists)
rows.standfirst: If we still measured inflation the way we did in 1980, today’s inflation rate would be 8%, Summers calculates.

rows.title: Britain has the most ‘fragile firms’ in Europe, with 15% of small and medium businesses at risk of default, Allianz says
rows.standfirst: The figures follow official data showing the U.K. slipped into a recession at the end of last year, with many analysts expecting stagnation for the next year.

rows.title: Goldman says office buildings need a 50% price drop for residential conversion to be a real thing
rows.standfirst: Office-to-residential conversions can be costly and take longer than new construction.

rows.title: Brooklyn’s new borough president doesn’t care about the ‘character’ of your neighborhood. That’s ‘not more important than putting people in homes’
rows.standfirst: When a city is missing hundreds of thousands of much-needed homes, the “character of your neighborhood,” an obsession that’s existed for generations, shouldn’t matter.

rows.title: The Silicon Valley billionaires’ astroturf city being built from scratch is running headlong into a NIMBY backlash
rows.standfirst: Former Goldman Sachs trader Jan Sramek unveiled his ballot initiative for “California Forever” in January but it’s not on the ballot yet.

rows.title: ‘A speed bump rather than pothole’: Key inflation report rankles Fed’s interest rate cut plans
rows.standfirst: The Fed’s favorite inflation gauge jumped 0.4% in January, but Capital Economics argues: “There is still plenty of disinflation coming this year.”

rows.title: 9 million homes will come on the market in the next decade as baby boomers age—but the ‘silver tsunami’ will be more of a ‘tide,’ Freddie Mac says
rows.standfirst: Baby boomers aren’t ready to give up their low or non-existent mortgage rates, but as they age their homeownership rates will decline, bringing more supply onto the market.
